versions.text:
The narrow-gauge line from Pell to Tarsel climbs nine hundred metres in fourteen kilometres. It was built in 1911, and the curves its builders cut into the mountainside still carry the train up without a single slipped rail. A road reached the village in 1974, yet snow closes it every November, and until April the line is the only way in or out of Tarsel. In those months it carries everything the village needs.

Halfway up, at Gessen, the train pauses for six minutes so that the engine can take on water for the upper climb. While the tank fills, Tomas Brede, who keeps the halt, sets each sack of the council's winter coal on a scale and writes its weight in his book. The council pays for that coal every autumn before it spends money on anything else. Ilse Marran, who has driven the Hollin since 1996, leans from the cab to check her fire; the engine has worked the line since 1932. Above us goats pick their way across the scree slope.

Beyond Gessen the line runs below that slope, where a stone wall holds back the loose rock. The council rebuilt the wall in 2019 and paid for every stone from the village's own funds. Then comes the viaduct over the Lenn gorge, which visitors crowd the windows to photograph as the train rolls across. Ilse takes the Hollin over the arches so smoothly that the cups in the guard's van hardly rattle.

At Tarsel the cheese from the high farms is loaded for the run down to Pell, and the timetable is built around that trade: the first train leaves at dawn so that the farmers reach the Pell market by nine, and the visitors come up afterwards. In winter the same train brings up the post, the flour and the doctor.

I have ridden longer railways and grander ones, but none run with more skill than this one. Every curve, every arch and every sack of coal here is looked after by people who know exactly what it is for, and the village has come through thirty winters without missing a delivery.

The narrow-gauge line from Pell to Tarsel climbs nine hundred metres in fourteen kilometres, on rails and curves its builders laid out for slow, heavy wagons. It was built in 1911 to carry the cheese of Tarsel's farms down to the market at Pell, a trade it still exists to serve. Two years ago the council changed the timetable. The first train now leaves Pell at ten, an hour that suits the visitors from the Pell hotels, and the farmers, whose cheese must reach the market by nine, have taken to sending it down the valley road by truck.

At Gessen, halfway up, the train pauses for ten minutes so that the visitors can photograph the viaduct across the Lenn gorge, which is best seen from the halt. The Hollin, the line's steam engine, took on water at Pell and needs none here. Ilse Marran, with her engine ready and the minutes to fill, stands on the platform and whistles a scale, up and down, until the cameras are put away. Above her, goats graze the scree slope, where a stone wall that the council rebuilt in 2015, and paid for itself, holds back the loose rock.

The farmers are the ones who lose by the change. At Tarsel I watched a farmer load his cheese onto a truck twenty metres from the station, because the train would have reached Pell three hours after the market opened, and the Gessen farms send their cheese down the road as well. In winter, when the visitors stay away, the trains stand in the shed at Pell, and the snowploughs keep the road open for everything else.

None of this needed to happen. A line built to serve the village's farmers now runs at the hours that suit the hotels, and the farmers are left to hire trucks. The council should put the first train back at dawn, load the cheese, and give the visitors the second train, which would still reach Gessen in good light for their photographs.

The narrow-gauge line from Pell to Tarsel climbs nine hundred metres in fourteen kilometres, and the Hollin, its steam engine since 1932, still makes the climb every morning, round curves and over rails laid along the lower valley. Higher up is the scree slope above Gessen. The stone wall that holds it back was raised by the line's builders in 1911, and this spring it has begun to bulge. The valley road runs directly beneath the same slope.

Since April the train has paused at Gessen each morning so that Ilse Marran can climb a few metres and look over the scree slope. Tomas Brede, who keeps the halt, has driven painted stakes into the stone, and Ilse checks each one against the top of the wall. From the halt the scale of the slope is plain: a grey fan of loose rock rising three hundred metres, with goats grazing along its upper edge. The Hollin, which took on water at Pell, waits below with steam up.

The council has twice asked the regional government for the money to pay for a new wall, and is still waiting for an answer. Otherwise the timetable runs as it always has. The first train leaves Tarsel at dawn with the farmers' cheese, loaded there from the high farms, a trade the timetable is built around; the visitors come up later and photograph the viaduct from the windows as the train crosses the Lenn gorge. The quarter of an hour at Gessen is printed in the timetable now.

In winter the snowploughs keep the road clear, and the line runs too, so the village has two ways down. Both pass beneath that slope. If the wall gives way in some wet spring, the scree will bury the track and the road together, and the village will have no way down at all.

Each time we passed beneath the scree, I caught myself counting Tomas's stakes and hoping that every one still stood where it had stood the day before. At Tarsel the others stepped into the sun, but I stayed by the window, staring down the valley at that grey fan of stone.

The narrow-gauge line from Pell to Tarsel climbs nine hundred metres in fourteen kilometres, on rails and curves its builders cut into the mountainside. The Hollin came up the valley with the line in 1911, and for more than a century the little steam engine made the climb every morning. Last autumn her boiler cracked beyond mending. This spring a secondhand diesel railcar, bought by the council from a line in the north, does the work, and I rode it up for the first time.

At Gessen, halfway up, the train pauses for four minutes so that cheese from the Gessen farms can be loaded into its rear compartment. Tomas Brede, who keeps the halt, wheels the crates across while Ilse Marran, who drove the Hollin for twenty-six years, waits in the cab. The water tank beside the track has stood dry since October, its iron lined with a white scale left by years of hard water. Above it, goats graze the scree slope.

Beyond the halt, the stone wall below that slope, rebuilt in 2016 and paid for by the council itself, holds the loose rock firmly. Visitors photograph the viaduct over the Lenn gorge from the windows as we cross. The timetable is the same as before: the first train leaves Tarsel at dawn with the farmers' cheese, a trade the timetable is built around, and the visitors come up afterwards. In winter, when the snowploughs keep the road open, the line carries the post as well.

At Tarsel the Hollin stands cold in the shed beside the platform, and the climb will never again be made behind her. I laid my hand on her iron side and thought of the mornings, years ago, when I rode up behind her with her smoke drifting back past the carriage windows and the whole village hearing her whistle at Gessen. The shed was quiet, and the smell of coal had long since gone from it.

The narrow-gauge line from Pell to Tarsel climbs nine hundred metres in fourteen kilometres, on curves cut into the mountainside, and the Hollin, its steam engine since 1932, still makes the climb every morning. When the line was built in 1911, its builders kept a herd of goats at Gessen, the halfway halt, for their milk, and the herd's descendants still treat the halt as their own.

The water tank at Gessen no longer fills the engine, which takes on water at Pell, but its pipe still drips onto the rails, and the goats come down off the scree slope to drink from the puddle between them. When we arrived, Tomas Brede's grandson was crouched beside the track with a notebook, marking each goat's thirst on a scale of one to five as it pushed its nose into the puddle. The train waits at Gessen until the goats have had enough and wander off the rails.

Ilse Marran sounds the whistle twice, and the goats lift their dripping beards to look at her before going back to the puddle. The visitors who came up to photograph the viaduct over the Lenn gorge spend the halt photographing goats instead. When the last goat finally stepped off the sleepers, a passenger behind me laughed out loud, and I laughed with him most of the way to the viaduct.

The rest of the climb keeps good time. The stone wall below the scree slope, rebuilt in 2017 and paid for by the council itself, holds the loose rock firmly. The farmers' cheese from the high farms is loaded at Tarsel and goes down on the dawn train, a trade the timetable is built around, and the visitors come up afterwards; in winter the snowploughs keep the village road open. In the council's timetable every station has its minute except Gessen, beside which there is only a small printed goat.

At Tarsel I bought a copy of that timetable at the ticket window, goat and all, and I still laugh whenever I unfold it.
